board-squares.prompt: How many squares does a chessboard have?
board-squares.explanation: 8 ranks × 8 files = 64 squares, alternating light and dark.

board-corner.prompt: With the board set up correctly, what color is the square in your bottom-right corner?
board-corner.explanation: Remember "light on the right". If that corner is dark, the board is turned the wrong way.

queen-own-color.prompt: Where does the white queen start?
queen-own-color.explanation: The queen goes on her own color: the white queen on d1 (light), the black queen on d8 (dark).

who-moves-first.prompt: Who makes the first move in a game?
who-moves-first.explanation: White always moves first, then the players take turns.

value-queen.prompt: Roughly how many points is a queen worth?
value-queen.explanation: Rough values: pawn 1, knight 3, bishop 3, rook 5, queen 9. The king is priceless — losing it loses the game.

value-rook.prompt: Roughly how many points is a rook worth?
value-rook.explanation: About 5 points — stronger than a knight or bishop (3) but weaker than a queen (9).

value-minor.prompt: How do a knight and a bishop compare in value?

choices.knight: A knight is worth two bishops

value-minor.explanation: Both are worth about 3. Bishops shine in open positions, knights in closed ones.

knight-jumps.prompt: Which piece can jump over other pieces?
knight-jumps.explanation: Only the knight moves in an L-shape and jumps over pieces.

bishop-color.prompt: Can a bishop move to a square of the other color?

choices.same: No, it always stays on one color

bishop-color.explanation: Bishops only move diagonally, so they stay on the same color all game.

pawn-backward.explanation: Pawns only move forward — think before you push them!

pawn-two-steps.prompt: When may a pawn move two squares at once?

choices.first: Only on that pawn's first move

pawn-two-steps.explanation: Each pawn may move two squares only on its first move, then one square at a time.

kings-adjacent.prompt: Can the two kings stand next to each other?
kings-adjacent.explanation: No. A king would be moving into a square attacked by the other king, which is illegal.

sq-knight-center.prompt: Click every square the knight on e4 can move to.
sq-knight-center.explanation: The knight moves in an L: two squares one way, then one to the side. In the center it has 8 moves.

sq-knight-corner.prompt: Which squares can the knight in the a1 corner reach?
sq-knight-corner.explanation: In the corner it has only 2 moves. As the saying goes: "a knight on the rim is dim".

sq-bishop.prompt: Click every square the bishop on d4 can move to.
sq-bishop.explanation: The bishop moves diagonally any distance, as long as nothing is in the way.

sq-rook.prompt: Click every square the rook on d4 can move to.
sq-rook.explanation: The rook moves along ranks and files any distance if the path is clear.

sq-queen.prompt: Click every square the queen on d4 can move to.
sq-queen.explanation: The queen combines rook and bishop: straight or diagonal, any distance.

sq-king.prompt: Click every square the king on d4 can move to.
sq-king.explanation: The king moves one square in any direction.

sq-pawn-start.prompt: Which squares can the pawn on e2 move to?
sq-pawn-start.explanation: On its first move a pawn may go one square (e3) or two (e4).

sq-pawn-capture.prompt: Which squares can the white pawn on e4 move to?
sq-pawn-capture.explanation: Pawns move straight but capture diagonally. e5 is blocked by the knight, but the pawn can capture on d5 or f5.

sq-escape-check.prompt: The white king is in check. Which squares can it escape to?
sq-escape-check.explanation: The rook on e8 controls the whole e-file, so e2 is still in check. The king must step to the d- or f-file.

mv-castle-short.explanation: Kingside castling: the king moves two squares right (e1 → g1) and the rook jumps to f1. Drag the king to g1.

mv-castle-long.explanation: Queenside castling: the king moves two squares left (e1 → c1) and the rook goes from a1 to d1.

mv-en-passant.prompt: Black just played d7 → d5. Capture en passant!
mv-en-passant.explanation: The e5 pawn captures diagonally to d6, taking the d5 pawn as if it had moved only one square. It must be done right away.

mv-promote.prompt: Promote the pawn to a queen.
mv-promote.explanation: A pawn reaching the last rank becomes a queen, rook, bishop or knight — almost always a queen.

mv-mate-back-rank.explanation: Rd8 is checkmate! Black's own pawns block the king's escape — a back-rank mate.

mv-mate-queen.explanation: Qh8 checks along the 8th rank, and the white king on b6 covers a7 and b7. No escape.

mv-fork.prompt: Find the knight move that attacks both the black king and rook.
mv-fork.explanation: Nc7+ checks the king and attacks the rook on a8 — a fork. Black must save the king and loses the rook.

mv-hanging.prompt: The black queen is undefended. Take it!
mv-hanging.explanation: Rd5 wins the queen for free. Always look for undefended ("hanging") enemy pieces.

mv-escape-check.prompt: The rook is checking your king. Get the king out of check.
mv-escape-check.explanation: The rook controls the first rank, so d1 and f1 are unsafe. Step up to d2 or e2.

castle-in-check.prompt: Which statement about castling is NOT true?

choices.unmoved: The king and rook must not have moved
choices.empty: The squares between them must be empty
choices.inCheck: You may castle while in check
choices.notThrough: The king may not pass through an attacked square

castle-in-check.explanation: You can't castle out of check, through check, or into check.

castle-king-moved.prompt: The king moved and came back to its square. Can it still castle?
castle-king-moved.explanation: Once the king has moved, castling is lost for good — even if it returns.

en-passant-timing.prompt: When can you capture en passant?

choices.immediately: Only on the very next move

en-passant-timing.explanation: Only immediately after the enemy pawn's two-square move. Miss it and the chance is gone.

promotion-pieces.prompt: What can a pawn promote to?
promotion-pieces.explanation: Queen, rook, bishop or knight — never a king. You can have two queens.

stalemate-result.prompt: Black to move is not in check but has no legal moves. What's the result?
stalemate-result.explanation: Stalemate is a draw. When you're winning big, be careful not to stalemate your opponent!

check-meaning.explanation: Check means the king is attacked, and it must be dealt with immediately.

choices.noEscape: The king is in check and cannot escape
choices.noMoves: No moves left but not in check

checkmate-meaning.explanation: Checkmate: the king is in check and can't move away, block or capture the attacker. That side loses.

draw-threefold.prompt: How many times must a position repeat for a draw?
draw-threefold.explanation: The same position three times (same side to move) is a draw.

draw-fifty.prompt: How many moves without a capture or pawn move lead to a draw?
draw-fifty.explanation: The fifty-move rule: 50 moves by each side with no capture and no pawn move.

draw-insufficient.prompt: Which is a draw by insufficient material?
draw-insufficient.explanation: A king and a single bishop cannot checkmate. A queen or rook can.

notation-square.prompt: In the square name "e4", what do the letter and number mean?
notation-square.explanation: The letter (a–h) is the file (column), the number (1–8) is the rank (row).

notation-capture.explanation: "x" means a capture: Nxe5 = knight takes on e5.

notation-check-mate.prompt: Which symbols mean check and checkmate?
notation-check-mate.explanation: "+" is check, "#" is checkmate. "!" praises a good move.

notation-castle.explanation: O-O is kingside castling, O-O-O is queenside castling.

notation-knight.prompt: Which letter stands for the knight in English notation?
notation-knight.explanation: N for kNight, because K is the King. This app shows piece icons (♘), so you don't need the letters.

opening-center.prompt: What should you prioritize in the opening?

choices.center: Control the center (d4, e4, d5, e5)

opening-center.explanation: Central pieces control more squares and can switch to either side quickly.

opening-develop.prompt: Which pieces should you develop first?
opening-develop.explanation: Bring out knights and bishops first. An early queen gets chased around and wastes time.

choices.safety: King safety and connecting the rooks

opening-castle.explanation: Castling takes the king out of the dangerous center and connects the rooks.

tactic-fork.prompt: One piece attacking two enemy pieces at once is called…
tactic-fork.explanation: A fork threatens two targets; the opponent can only save one.

tactic-pin.prompt: A piece can't (or shouldn't) move because it would expose a more valuable piece behind it. That's…
tactic-pin.explanation: A pin: the front piece is stuck because the piece behind is worth more (often the king or queen).

tactic-skewer.prompt: Attacking a valuable piece so that when it moves, the piece behind it falls. That's…
tactic-skewer.explanation: A skewer is a reverse pin: the more valuable piece is in front and must move away.

sq-knight-jump-wall.prompt: The knight on e4 is surrounded by pawns. Where can it still go?
sq-knight-jump-wall.explanation: Knights jump over pieces, so the wall of pawns does not stop it: all 8 squares are available.

sq-bishop-blocked.prompt: Which squares can the bishop on c2 move to?
sq-bishop-blocked.explanation: Your own pawns on b3 and d3 block both forward diagonals, so the bishop can only go back to b1 or d1.

sq-rook-captures.prompt: Which squares can the rook on d4 reach (including captures)?
sq-rook-captures.explanation: The rook stops when it captures an enemy piece (d6, f4) and is blocked by your own pawn on b4.

sq-queen-corner.prompt: Which squares can the queen in the a1 corner reach?
sq-queen-corner.explanation: From the corner the queen goes up the a-file, right as far as d1 (the king on e1 blocks), and along the long a1–h8 diagonal.

sq-king-corner.prompt: Which squares can the king in the h1 corner move to?
sq-king-corner.explanation: In the corner the king has only 3 squares: g1, g2 and h2.

sq-pawn-blocked.prompt: The e2 pawn is blocked by a knight. Where can it go?
sq-pawn-blocked.explanation: It cannot move straight because e3 is occupied, but it can still capture the bishop on d3 diagonally.

knight-color-change.prompt: After each move, what color square is the knight on compared to before?
knight-color-change.explanation: A knight always changes color: light to dark, dark to light.

pawns-per-side.prompt: How many pawns does each side start with?
pawns-per-side.explanation: Each side has 8 pawns, filling the 2nd rank (White) or the 7th rank (Black).

queen-combines.prompt: The queen moves like a combination of which two pieces?

king-no-value.prompt: Why does the king have no point value like the other pieces?
king-no-value.explanation: Losing the king loses the game, so it can never be traded for anything.

rooks-start.explanation: The four rooks start in the four corners: a1, h1, a8, h8.

bishops-colors.prompt: What colors do one side's two bishops move on?
bishops-colors.explanation: One bishop is on light squares, the other on dark squares — they never meet.

mv-block-with-queen.prompt: The black rook checks along the first rank. Block the check with your queen.
mv-block-with-queen.explanation: Putting the queen on d1 or c1 blocks the rook.

mv-capture-knight-check.prompt: The black knight is giving check. Capture the checking piece.
mv-capture-knight-check.explanation: Bxf3: the bishop takes the knight and the check is gone.

sq-escape-rank.prompt: The black rook checks along the first rank. Where can the king go?
sq-escape-rank.explanation: The whole first rank is covered by the rook, so the king must step up to d2, e2 or f2.

sq-king-castling.prompt: Click every square the king on e1 can reach — castling included!
sq-king-castling.explanation: Besides the 5 squares around it, the king can castle to g1 or c1.

castle-through-attack.prompt: The f1 square is attacked. May White castle kingside?
castle-through-attack.explanation: No. The king may not pass through an attacked square while castling.

castle-rook-attacked.prompt: The h1 rook is attacked (the king is not). May White castle kingside?
castle-rook-attacked.explanation: Yes! The rule only cares about the king’s squares. An attacked rook can still castle.

castle-b1-attacked.prompt: For queenside castling, b1 is attacked (c1 and d1 are not). Is castling allowed?
castle-b1-attacked.explanation: Yes. The king only crosses d1 and lands on c1; b1 just has to be empty for the rook.

stalemate-corner.prompt: Black to move. What is the result?
stalemate-corner.explanation: The black king is not in check, but a7, b7 and b8 are all covered by the queen: stalemate.

recognize-mate.prompt: Black to move. What is this position?
recognize-mate.explanation: The a8 rook gives check and Black’s own pawns block every escape: checkmate.

promotion-rank.prompt: Which rank does a white pawn promote on?
promotion-rank.explanation: White pawns promote on the 8th rank; black pawns on the 1st.

en-passant-who.prompt: Which pieces can capture en passant?
en-passant-who.explanation: Only pawns can capture en passant, and only pawns can be captured that way.

draw-by-agreement.prompt: Can the players agree to a draw?
draw-by-agreement.explanation: Yes. One player offers a draw; if the other accepts, the game is drawn.

ignore-check.prompt: When in check, may you make a move that ignores the check?
ignore-check.explanation: No. Any move that leaves your king in check is illegal.

fifty-move-reset.explanation: A capture or a pawn move resets the fifty-move count.

choices.captureOrPawn: A capture or a pawn move

mv-mate-smothered.explanation: Nf7#: a smothered mate! The black king is boxed in by its own pieces and has nowhere to go.

mv-mate-two-rooks.explanation: Rb8#: the a7 rook locks the 7th rank and the other rook checks on the 8th — the "ladder" mate.

mv-mate-queen-king.explanation: Qe7#: the queen goes right next to the enemy king, protected by your own king.

mv-mate-arabian.explanation: Rg8#: the f6 knight protects the rook and covers h7 — the classic "Arabian" mate.

mv-mate-back-rank-queen.explanation: Qe8#: the black king is stuck behind its own pawns — a back-rank mate.

mv-mate-h7.explanation: Qxh7#: the d3 bishop protects the queen, so the king cannot take it and has no escape.

mv-mate-promote.explanation: a8=Q#: promotion with a back-rank mate!

mv-mate-rook-king.explanation: Ra8#: the white king covers g7 and h7; the rook checks along the 8th rank.

mv-fork-queen-knight.prompt: Use your knight to fork the black king and queen.
mv-fork-queen-knight.explanation: Ne7+: the knight checks the g8 king and attacks the c6 queen. Black must move the king and loses the queen.

mv-fork-pawn.prompt: Even a pawn can fork. Attack both knights at once!
mv-fork-pawn.explanation: d5: the pawn attacks both the c6 and e6 knights; Black can only save one.

mv-fork-queen.prompt: Use your queen to check the king and attack the rook at the same time.
mv-fork-queen.explanation: Qd5+: the queen checks the g8 king on one diagonal and hits the a8 rook on the other.

mv-skewer-rook.prompt: The black king and queen are on the same file. Skewer them!
mv-skewer-rook.explanation: Re1+: the king has to leave the e-file, and then the rook takes the queen on e8.

mv-skewer-bishop.prompt: The black king and rook are on the same diagonal. Skewer them with your bishop!
mv-skewer-bishop.explanation: Bf3+: the d5 king must leave the diagonal, and then the bishop takes the a8 rook.

mv-pin-knight.prompt: Pin the black knight to its king.
mv-pin-knight.explanation: Bb5: the d7 knight stands between the bishop and the king, so it cannot move — an absolute pin.

mv-take-hanging-bishop.prompt: The black bishop is undefended. Take it!
mv-take-hanging-bishop.explanation: Nxc5: the c5 bishop was hanging and nobody can recapture.

tactic-discovered.prompt: A piece moves away and opens a line for the piece behind it. What is this tactic called?
tactic-discovered.explanation: It is a discovered attack. If the piece behind gives check, it is a discovered check.

tactic-double-check.prompt: In a double check (two pieces giving check), what is the only way out?
tactic-double-check.explanation: You cannot block or capture two checkers at once, so the king must move.

tactic-deflection.prompt: Forcing an enemy defender to abandon its defensive duty is called what?
tactic-deflection.explanation: That is a deflection: lure the defender away, then attack what it was guarding.

tactic-hanging.explanation: A hanging piece is attacked and undefended — it can be taken for free.

choices.undefended: An attacked piece with no defender

tactic-smothered-piece.prompt: A smothered mate (king boxed in by its own pieces) is usually delivered by which piece?
tactic-smothered-piece.explanation: The knight — because it can jump over the pieces surrounding the king.

tactic-back-rank.prompt: Your king has castled and the three pawns in front have not moved. What is the danger?
tactic-back-rank.explanation: The king has no escape square on the 2nd rank, so an enemy rook or queen on your back rank can mate.

tactic-pinned-move.prompt: A piece is absolutely pinned (the king is behind it). May it leave the pin line?
tactic-pinned-move.explanation: No. Moving it would expose the king to check, which is illegal.

tactic-fork-piece.prompt: Which piece is most famous for forks?
tactic-fork-piece.explanation: The knight: it attacks up to 8 squares in an L-shape and cannot be blocked.

nt-play-e4.explanation: No piece letter means a pawn: the pawn goes to e4.

nt-play-nf3.explanation: N is the knight: the g1 knight jumps to f3.

nt-play-bc4.explanation: B is the bishop: the f1 bishop goes diagonally to c4.

nt-play-oo.explanation: O-O is kingside castling: the king goes to g1 and the rook to f1.

nt-play-ooo.explanation: O-O-O is queenside castling: the king goes to c1 and the rook to d1.

nt-play-exd5.explanation: For a pawn capture we write its starting file, then "x": the e-pawn captures on d5.

nt-play-nxe5.explanation: "x" means a capture: the knight takes the pawn on e5.

nt-play-promote.explanation: "=Q" means promoting to a queen, "+" means check.

nt-play-nbd2.explanation: Both knights can reach d2, so the "b" tells you it is the knight on the b-file.

nt-play-rfe1.explanation: Both rooks can reach e1; the "f" points to the rook on the f-file.

nt-play-qh5-mate.explanation: "#" means checkmate: the queen goes to h5 and the game is over!

nt-play-bxf7.explanation: The bishop captures on f7 and gives check.

nt-files.prompt: How are the files (left to right from White's side) labelled?
nt-files.explanation: Files are labelled with the letters a to h.

nt-ranks.prompt: Which side is the 1st rank on?
nt-ranks.explanation: The 1st rank is on White's side; the 8th rank on Black's.

nt-promo-symbol.explanation: A pawn moves to e8 and promotes to a queen.

choices.promote: A pawn reaches e8 and becomes a queen

nt-good-move.prompt: What does "!" after a move mean?
nt-good-move.explanation: "!" is a good move, "!!" a brilliant one.

nt-blunder.prompt: What does "??" after a move mean?
nt-blunder.explanation: "??" is a blunder; "?" is a mistake.

nt-dubious.explanation: "?!" is a dubious move; "!?" on the other hand is an interesting one.

nt-result-white.explanation: 1-0: White wins; 0-1: Black wins; ½-½: draw.

nt-result-draw.explanation: Each side gets half a point: the game is a draw.

nt-pgn.explanation: PGN (Portable Game Notation) is a text file format for recording whole games.

nt-black-move-number.explanation: The "..." tells you it is Black’s move in move 12.

str-early-queen.prompt: Why should you not bring the queen out too early?
str-early-queen.explanation: Enemy minor pieces will chase it while developing — you lose time.

choices.chased: It gets chased and you lose time
choices.weak: The queen is a weak piece

str-move-twice.prompt: In the opening, should you move the same piece several times?
str-move-twice.explanation: Avoid it unless necessary: each move should develop a new piece.

str-rook-open-file.prompt: Where is a rook most active?
str-rook-open-file.explanation: On an open file (no pawns), the rook controls the whole file and can invade.

str-rook-seventh.prompt: A white rook reaches Black's 7th rank. How is that usually?
str-rook-seventh.explanation: Very strong: it attacks unmoved pawns and traps the king on the back rank.

str-bishop-pair.prompt: When is the bishop pair usually strongest?
str-bishop-pair.explanation: In open positions with clear diagonals — the two bishops cover both light and dark squares.

str-knight-rim.prompt: "A knight on the rim is dim." Why?
str-knight-rim.explanation: On the edge a knight controls only 2–4 squares instead of 8 in the center.

str-passed-pawn.explanation: A pawn with no enemy pawns blocking or guarding its path to promotion.

choices.noBlockers: A pawn no enemy pawn can stop

str-doubled-pawns.prompt: Two pawns of the same color on one file (doubled pawns) are usually what?
str-doubled-pawns.explanation: Usually a weakness: they cannot protect each other and are hard to advance.

str-isolated-pawn.explanation: A pawn with no friendly pawns on the neighbouring files, so no pawn can defend it.

choices.noNeighbours: No friendly pawns on adjacent files

str-king-endgame.prompt: In the endgame (few pieces left), what should the king do?
str-king-endgame.explanation: Come forward and help! With few pieces left, the king is a strong fighting piece.

str-trade-when-ahead.prompt: When you are ahead in material, what should you trade?
str-trade-when-ahead.explanation: Trade pieces (not pawns): the fewer pieces left, the clearer your advantage.

str-outpost.prompt: What is an "outpost" for a knight?
str-outpost.explanation: A square in enemy territory that enemy pawns can never attack, usually supported by your own pawn.

choices.noPawnAttack: A square enemy pawns cannot attack
choices.kingSide: A square next to your king

str-center-squares.prompt: Which are the four center squares?
str-center-squares.explanation: d4, e4, d5, e5 — controlling them makes your pieces more active.

str-castle-early.explanation: Early, once a few pieces are developed — the king is safe and the rook joins the game.

str-rook-behind-passer.prompt: Where should a rook stand relative to a passed pawn?
str-rook-behind-passer.explanation: Behind the passed pawn (yours or the enemy’s): the rook gets more active as the pawn advances.

str-opposition.prompt: The kings face each other with one square between them and the other side must move. What is this called?
str-opposition.explanation: It is the opposition — very important in pawn endgames.

str-bad-bishop.explanation: A bishop hemmed in by its own pawns standing on its square color.

choices.ownPawns: Blocked by its own pawns on its color

str-exchange.prompt: What does "giving up the exchange" mean?
str-exchange.explanation: Giving a rook (5) for a bishop or knight (3) — a loss of 2 points.

choices.rookForMinor: A rook for a bishop or knight

str-rule-of-square.prompt: What is the "rule of the square" used for?
str-rule-of-square.explanation: To quickly see whether a king can catch a passed pawn before it promotes.

choices.catchPawn: Can the king catch a passed pawn?

str-fianchetto.explanation: Developing a bishop to b2/g2 (or b7/g7) so it controls the long diagonal.

choices.longDiagonal: A bishop on b2/g2 on the long diagonal

str-king-shelter.prompt: After castling, what should you do with the three pawns in front of your king?
str-king-shelter.explanation: Keep them in place as long as you can — they are the king’s shield.

str-opposite-bishops.prompt: An endgame with opposite-colored bishops (one light-squared, one dark-squared) usually ends how?
str-opposite-bishops.explanation: Often in a draw, even a pawn or two down: the bishops never fight over the same squares.

choices.winning: Easy win for the side a pawn up

str-mv-develop.prompt: Develop a minor piece (knight or bishop).
str-mv-develop.explanation: For example Nf3, Nc3 or Bc4: bringing out the minor pieces comes first in the opening.

str-mv-castle-safety.prompt: Your king is still in the center. Bring it to safety.
str-mv-castle-safety.explanation: O-O: the king tucks behind its pawns and the f1 rook is ready to fight.

str-mv-center-pawn.prompt: First move: occupy the center with a pawn.
str-mv-center-pawn.explanation: e4 or d4: the pawn takes the center and opens lines for the queen and bishop.

str-mv-rook-open-file.prompt: The d- and e-files have no pawns. Put a rook on an open file.
str-mv-rook-open-file.explanation: For example Rfe1 or Rad1: a rook on an open file controls the whole file.

str-mv-king-endgame.prompt: A pawn endgame. Bring your king toward the center.
str-mv-king-endgame.explanation: Ke2 or Kd2: in the endgame the king must become active.

sq-rook-h1.prompt: Click every square the rook on h1 can move to.
sq-rook-h1.explanation: The rook runs up the h-file and left as far as f1 — the king on e1 is in the way.

sq-bishop-a3.prompt: Click every square the bishop on a3 can move to.
sq-bishop-a3.explanation: From a3 the bishop has two diagonals: up to f8 and down to c1.

sq-knight-h4.prompt: Click every square the knight on h4 can move to.
sq-knight-h4.explanation: On the edge the knight has only 4 squares: g6, f5, f3, g2.

sq-knight-b1-start.prompt: Click every square the knight on b1 can move to.
sq-knight-b1-start.explanation: In the starting position the b1 knight jumps over the pawns to a3 or c3.

sq-pawn-e2-blocked-e4.prompt: Click every square the pawn on e2 can move to.
sq-pawn-e2-blocked-e4.explanation: The pawn would like to go two squares, but e4 is occupied, so only e3 is possible.

sq-pawn-black-d7.prompt: Click every square the pawn on d7 can move to.
sq-pawn-black-d7.explanation: Black pawns move down toward rank 1. On its first move it can go one or two squares: d6, d5.

sq-queen-d1-open.prompt: Click every square the queen on d1 can move to.
sq-queen-d1-open.explanation: After 1.e4 e5 the d1–h5 diagonal opens: the queen can go to e2, f3, g4, h5.

sq-bishop-f1-open.prompt: Click every square the bishop on f1 can move to.
sq-bishop-f1-open.explanation: With the e-pawn gone, the f1 bishop has the whole diagonal to a6.

sq-king-opposition.prompt: Click every square the king on e4 can move to.
sq-king-opposition.explanation: The two kings may never stand next to each other, so d5, e5 and f5 are off-limits.

sq-rook-pinned-file.prompt: Click every square the rook on e2 can move to.
sq-rook-pinned-file.explanation: The e2 rook is pinned to its king: it may only move along the e-file, including taking on e8.

sq-bishop-pinned-diag.prompt: Click every square the bishop on d2 can move to.
sq-bishop-pinned-diag.explanation: The d2 bishop is pinned by the b4 bishop: it may only move along the pin — c3 or take on b4.

sq-pawn-promote-three.prompt: Click every square the pawn on b7 can move to.
sq-pawn-promote-three.explanation: The b7 pawn can go straight to b8 or capture on a8 or c8 — each one is a promotion!

sq-king-castle-one-side.prompt: Click every square the king on e1 can move to.
sq-king-castle-one-side.explanation: The f1 bishop blocks the kingside, so the king can only castle queenside (c1).

sq-pawn-en-passant.prompt: Click every square the pawn on e5 can move to.
sq-pawn-en-passant.explanation: The d-pawn just moved two squares past the e5 pawn, so it can capture en passant on d6.

sq-queen-blockers.prompt: Click every square the queen on e4 can move to.
sq-queen-blockers.explanation: The queen stops at enemy pieces (c6, e6, g4 — capturable) and before its own (c4, e2).

knight-max-moves.prompt: What is the most moves a knight can have?
knight-max-moves.explanation: In the middle of the board a knight has up to 8 L-shaped squares.

queen-max-squares.prompt: On an empty board, how many squares can a centralized queen control?
queen-max-squares.explanation: A queen on d4 or e4 controls 27 squares — more than any other piece.

rook-squares-always.prompt: On an empty board, how many squares does a rook always control?
rook-squares-always.explanation: Wherever it stands: 7 on its file + 7 on its rank = 14.

choices.depends: It depends on where it is

bishop-light-dark.prompt: Can a light-squared bishop ever reach a dark square?
bishop-light-dark.explanation: Never: moving diagonally keeps the same square color.

pawn-capture-direction.prompt: In which direction does a pawn capture?
pawn-capture-direction.explanation: A pawn moves straight but captures one square diagonally forward.

king-step.prompt: Apart from castling, how far can the king move in one turn?
king-step.explanation: The king moves one square in any direction; only castling moves it two.

pieces-total.prompt: How many pieces does each side start with in total?
pieces-total.explanation: 8 pawns + 2 rooks + 2 knights + 2 bishops + queen + king = 16.

knight-start-squares.explanation: The knights stand next to the rooks: b1 and g1 (Black: b8 and g8).

king-start-file.prompt: On which file do the kings start?
king-start-file.explanation: Both kings start on the e-file: e1 and e8.

value-pawn.prompt: About how many points is a pawn worth?
value-pawn.explanation: The pawn is the basic unit: 1 point.

two-rooks-vs-queen.prompt: By points, how do two rooks compare with a queen?
two-rooks-vs-queen.explanation: Two rooks = 10 points, queen = 9: the rooks are slightly more.

capture-own-piece.prompt: May you capture one of your own pieces?
capture-own-piece.explanation: No. You may only capture enemy pieces.

king-never-captured.prompt: Is the king ever captured and removed from the board?
king-never-captured.explanation: No. The game ends as soon as the king is checkmated, before it can be taken.

two-queens.prompt: Can one side have two queens at the same time?
two-queens.explanation: Yes! Promote a pawn to a queen while the first queen is still on the board.

pawn-first-move.prompt: How far must a pawn move on its first move?
pawn-first-move.explanation: Your choice: one or two squares.

mv-en-passant-black.prompt: Black to move. White just played e2–e4. Capture en passant!
mv-en-passant-black.explanation: dxe3 e.p.: the d4 pawn captures on e3 as if the white pawn had moved one square.

mv-underpromote-knight.prompt: Promote the pawn to a piece that checks the black king right away.
mv-underpromote-knight.explanation: d8=N+: a knight on d8 checks the f7 king. You do not always have to promote to a queen!

mv-castle-legal-side.prompt: Castle — but only one way is legal!
mv-castle-legal-side.explanation: The c4 bishop covers f1, so kingside castling is illegal. O-O-O is fine.

mv-king-takes-queen.prompt: The white king is in check. Get out of check.
mv-king-takes-queen.explanation: Kxe2: the queen is right next to the king and undefended, so the king can simply take it.

mv-block-with-knight.prompt: The black bishop gives check. Block it with your knight.
mv-block-with-knight.explanation: Nc3 or Nd2 steps onto the diagonal between the bishop and the king.

mv-promote-black.prompt: Black to move: promote the pawn to a queen.
mv-promote-black.explanation: a1=Q+: the black pawn reaches the 1st rank and becomes a queen.

mv-castle-black-short.explanation: O-O: the black king goes to g8 and the h8 rook to f8.

sq-escape-queen-e3.prompt: Click every square the king on e1 can move to.
sq-escape-queen-e3.explanation: The e3 queen covers d2, e2 and f2. The king only has d1 or f1.

sq-king-protected-rook.prompt: Click every square the king on e1 can move to.
sq-king-protected-rook.explanation: The d2 rook is protected by the d8 rook, so the king cannot take it; e2, f2 and d1 are covered. Only f1 is left.

sq-no-castle-through.prompt: Click every square the king on e1 can move to.
sq-no-castle-through.explanation: The f8 rook controls the whole f-file, so the king cannot go to f1 or f2 — and cannot castle either.

sq-en-passant-black.prompt: Click every square the pawn on d4 can move to.
sq-en-passant-black.explanation: The d4 pawn can go straight to d3, or capture en passant on e3.

sq-escape-knight-check.prompt: Click every square the king on e1 can move to.
sq-escape-knight-check.explanation: A knight check cannot be blocked, so the king must move. The d3 knight also covers f2, leaving d1, d2, e2, f1.

touch-move.prompt: Under the "touch-move" rule (over-the-board play), what happens if you deliberately touch one of your pieces?
touch-move.explanation: You must move that piece (if it has a legal move).

castle-once.prompt: How many times may each side castle in a game?

castle-rook-returned.prompt: The h1 rook moved and came back to h1. Can White still castle kingside?
castle-rook-returned.explanation: No. Once that rook has moved, castling on that side is gone for good.

castle-after-old-check.prompt: Your king was checked earlier and you blocked it (the king never moved). May you castle later?
castle-after-old-check.explanation: Yes. Castling is only forbidden while in check; an old check does not matter.

en-passant-optional.explanation: No — unless it happens to be the only legal move.

promotion-mandatory.prompt: When a pawn reaches the last rank, must it promote?
promotion-mandatory.explanation: Yes. A pawn can never stay a pawn on the last rank.

choices.no: No, it may stay a pawn

stalemate-vs-mate.prompt: What is the difference between stalemate and checkmate?
stalemate-vs-mate.explanation: In both there is no legal move, but in stalemate the king is not in check.

choices.notInCheck: In stalemate the king is not in check
choices.noPieces: In stalemate there are no pieces left

timeout-lone-king.prompt: Your time runs out, but your opponent has only a king. Result?
timeout-lone-king.explanation: A draw: your opponent cannot possibly checkmate you.

two-kings-only.prompt: Only the two kings are left. Result?
two-kings-only.explanation: An immediate draw: neither side can checkmate.

choices.continue: Play on until time runs out

king-knight-vs-king.prompt: King and knight against a lone king. Result?
king-knight-vs-king.explanation: A draw — one knight is not enough to checkmate.

choices.win: The side with the knight wins

threefold-not-consecutive.prompt: For a threefold repetition draw, must the repetitions be consecutive?
threefold-not-consecutive.explanation: No. The same position (same side to move) just has to appear three times in the game.

king-into-check.prompt: May the king move onto an attacked square?
king-into-check.explanation: No. The king may never put itself in check.

resign-meaning.prompt: What does it mean to resign?
resign-meaning.explanation: The player who resigns loses the game immediately.

flag-fall.prompt: Your clock runs out while your opponent still has enough material to mate. Result?

say-check.prompt: Do you have to say "check" when you give check?
say-check.explanation: No — your opponent has to notice it themselves.

seventy-five-moves.prompt: What happens after 75 moves by each side without a capture or pawn move?
seventy-five-moves.explanation: The game is drawn automatically, no claim needed (at 50 moves a player must claim it).

nt-play-d4.explanation: The d2 pawn advances two squares to d4.

nt-play-nc3.explanation: The b1 knight jumps to c3.

nt-play-c4.explanation: The English Opening: the c-pawn goes to c4.

nt-play-black-e5.explanation: "1..." means Black’s reply in move 1: the e7 pawn to e5.

nt-play-black-nf6.explanation: The Alekhine Defence: the g8 knight jumps to f6.

nt-play-black-c5.explanation: The Sicilian Defence: the c7 pawn advances to c5.

nt-play-bb5.explanation: The Ruy Lopez: the f1 bishop goes to b5, eyeing the c6 knight.

nt-play-qxd5.explanation: The black queen recaptures the pawn on d5.

nt-play-black-oo.explanation: Black castles kingside: king to g8, rook to f8.

nt-play-kd2.explanation: K is the king: the e1 king steps to d2.

nt-play-ra8-mate.explanation: Rook to a8 — "#" means it is a back-rank mate.

nt-play-exf6-ep.explanation: "e.p." stands for en passant: the e5 pawn captures onto f6.

nt-play-axb8n.explanation: The a7 pawn takes the knight on b8 and promotes to a knight.

nt-play-r1d3.explanation: Both rooks on the d-file can reach d3; the "1" points to the rook on the 1st rank.

nt-play-black-qh4-mate.explanation: The fastest possible checkmate — the "Fool’s Mate"!

nt-play-bxc6.explanation: The b5 bishop takes the c6 knight (the Exchange Variation of the Ruy Lopez).

nt-read-d5.explanation: The letter is the file, the number is the rank: d-file, 5th rank.

nt-h1-color.explanation: Each player's right-hand corner is always light — h1 is a light square.

nt-a1-color.explanation: a1 is dark (h1 is light, and colors alternate).

nt-ooo.explanation: Three O’s is queenside castling; two O’s is kingside castling.

nt-k-letter.explanation: K = king. (The knight uses N to avoid a clash.)

nt-r-letter.prompt: Which letter stands for the rook?

nt-no-letter.prompt: In the move "d4", which piece moves?
nt-no-letter.explanation: No piece letter means it is a pawn.

nt-fen.explanation: FEN is a single line of text describing one position (pieces, side to move, castling rights…).

nt-move-pair.prompt: In notation, what does one numbered move (e.g. "5.") contain?
nt-move-pair.explanation: One move by White and one by Black, e.g. "5. Nf3 Nc6".

choices.both: One White move + one Black move

nt-h-file.prompt: From White's side, which is the rightmost file?
nt-h-file.explanation: Left to right: a, b, c … h. The rightmost is the h-file.

nt-black-back-rank.prompt: On which rank do Black's pieces (not the pawns) start?
nt-black-back-rank.explanation: The 8th rank; the black pawns are on the 7th.

nt-white-pawn-rank.prompt: On which rank do the white pawns start?
nt-white-pawn-rank.explanation: The 2nd rank, right in front of the other pieces.

nt-why-nbd2.prompt: Why must you sometimes write "Nbd2" instead of "Nd2"?
nt-why-nbd2.explanation: Because both knights can reach d2; the "b" says which one moves.

nt-brilliant.explanation: "!!" marks a brilliant move — often a surprising sacrifice.

nt-zero-one.explanation: The left number is White's score: 0-1 means Black won.

str-mv-defend-e5.prompt: Black to move. The f3 knight attacks e5. Defend it by developing a knight.
str-mv-defend-e5.explanation: Nc6: it defends e5 and brings a minor piece into play at the same time.

str-mv-run-passed-pawn.prompt: The black king is far away. Push your passed pawn toward promotion.
str-mv-run-passed-pawn.explanation: The black king is outside the pawn’s “square”, so it cannot catch it — just run!

str-mv-rook-seventh.prompt: Put your rook on the opponent's 7th rank.
str-mv-rook-seventh.explanation: Rd7: a rook on the 7th attacks the pawns and keeps the black king on the back rank.

str-mv-knight-center.prompt: Your knight is on the rim. Bring it closer to the center.
str-mv-knight-center.explanation: Nb5 or Nc4: the closer to the center, the more squares the knight controls.

str-mv-fianchetto.prompt: The g-pawn is on g3. Complete the fianchetto.
str-mv-fianchetto.explanation: Bg2: the bishop sits on the long h1–a8 diagonal.

str-mv-rook-behind-passer.prompt: The a5 pawn is passed. Put your rook on the best square to support it.
str-mv-rook-behind-passer.explanation: Ra1: the rook stands behind the passed pawn and grows stronger as the pawn advances.

str-blockade.prompt: The square right in front of an enemy isolated pawn is ideal for which of your pieces?
str-blockade.explanation: A knight: it blocks the pawn and no pawn can chase it away.

str-tempo.explanation: A tempo is one move — a unit of time. "Losing a tempo" means wasting a move.

str-zugzwang.explanation: The side to move would be worse off after any move — they wish they could pass.

choices.anyMoveWorse: Having to move when every move hurts

str-open-bishop.prompt: In an open position (lots of open lines), which is usually stronger: bishop or knight?
str-open-bishop.explanation: The bishop — it thrives on long open diagonals.

str-closed-knight.prompt: In a closed position (locked pawn chains), which piece is usually stronger?
str-closed-knight.explanation: The knight — it hops over pawn chains while the bishop gets blocked.

str-chain-base.prompt: When attacking a pawn chain, where should you aim?
str-chain-base.explanation: At its base — the last pawn, which no pawn defends.

str-backward-pawn.explanation: A pawn left behind its neighbours: they cannot protect it and it is hard to advance.

str-pawn-majority.prompt: You have three pawns against two on the queenside. What is that majority for?
str-pawn-majority.explanation: Push them to create a passed pawn.

str-connected-passers.prompt: Two passed pawns side by side (connected) are usually…?
str-connected-passers.explanation: Very strong: they protect each other as they advance.

str-king-center-open-file.prompt: The e-file is open and your king is still on e1. How is that?
str-king-center-open-file.explanation: Dangerous: enemy rooks and queen can hit the king directly. Castle!

str-develop-first.prompt: What should you do before attacking?
str-develop-first.explanation: Develop your pieces and make your king safe — a one-piece attack usually fails.

choices.queen: Attack with the queen right away

str-knights-first.prompt: Rule of thumb: which pieces do you usually develop first in the opening?
str-knights-first.explanation: Knights before bishops — the best knight squares (f3, c3) are usually clear early.

str-poisoned-pawn.prompt: Grabbing the opponent’s b2 pawn with your queen early in the opening is usually…?
str-poisoned-pawn.explanation: Risky: the queen can get trapped in the corner and you lose many moves getting it out.

choices.risky: Risky — the queen can get trapped

str-weak-square.explanation: A square your pawns can never defend again — an enemy piece can settle there for good.

choices.noPawnCover: A square your pawns can no longer defend

str-trade-when-behind.prompt: When you are behind in material, how should you treat trades?
str-trade-when-behind.explanation: Avoid them: more pieces on the board means more counterplay.

str-rook-pawn-draw.prompt: King and a-pawn against king, with the defending king already in the a8 corner. Usual result?
str-rook-pawn-draw.explanation: A draw: the defending king cannot be driven out of the corner.

choices.win: The side with the pawn wins

str-lucena.prompt: The "Lucena position" in rook endings is famous for which technique?
str-lucena.explanation: "Building a bridge": the rook shields the king so the pawn can promote — a winning method.

str-philidor.prompt: What is the "Philidor position" in rook endings?
str-philidor.explanation: The standard drawing defence in rook and pawn vs rook: keep your rook on the 3rd rank.

str-kq-vs-k.prompt: King and queen against a lone king, played correctly. Result?
str-kq-vs-k.explanation: Always a win: queen and king drive the enemy king to the edge and mate (watch out for stalemate!).

str-kbn-vs-k.prompt: King, bishop and knight against a lone king?
str-kbn-vs-k.explanation: It is a win, but hard: drive the king into a corner of the bishop’s color within 50 moves.

str-two-knights.prompt: Can king and two knights force mate against a lone king?
str-two-knights.explanation: No — with correct defence, two knights cannot force checkmate.

str-improve-worst.prompt: There is no tactic in the position. What is a good plan?

str-ask-threat.prompt: After every move by your opponent, what should you ask first?
str-ask-threat.explanation: "What is my opponent threatening?" — look for checks, captures and threats.

choices.mine: Only think about my own plan

str-space.explanation: Your pawns are further up the board, giving your pieces more room to manoeuvre than the opponent’s.

mv-mate-queen-bishop-g7.explanation: Qg7#: the queen is protected by the b2 bishop along the long diagonal.

mv-mate-rook-knight.explanation: Ra8#: the f5 knight covers g7 and the rook checks along the 8th rank.

mv-mate-black-back-rank.explanation: Rd1#: the white king is trapped behind its own three pawns.

mv-mate-black-queen.explanation: Qf1#: the queen checks along the first rank and the g2/h2 pawns block the king’s escape.

mv-mate-queen-knight-g7.explanation: Qg7#: the f5 knight protects the queen, so the king cannot take it and has no square.

mv-mate-queen-rook-h-file.explanation: Qh2#: the g1 rook locks the g-file and the queen checks down the h-file.

mv-mate-pawn.explanation: g7#: even a pawn can deliver mate! The f7 king protects the pawn and covers g8.

mv-fork-two-rooks.prompt: Fork the two black rooks with your knight.
mv-fork-two-rooks.explanation: Nc5 attacks both the a6 and e6 rooks — Black loses one of them.

mv-skewer-bishop-queen.prompt: The black king and queen share a diagonal. Skewer them!
mv-skewer-bishop-queen.explanation: Bb3+: the f7 king has to move, then the bishop takes the queen on g8.

mv-pin-queen.prompt: Pin the black queen to its king.
mv-pin-queen.explanation: Bc4: the queen cannot leave the diagonal; if Qxc4 then bxc4 — Black gives the queen for a bishop.

mv-discovered-attack-queen.prompt: The e4 bishop is blocking the e1 rook. Use a discovered attack to win the queen!
mv-discovered-attack-queen.explanation: Bxa8+: the bishop takes the queen and uncovers the rook’s check — a discovered check.

mv-take-hanging-rook.prompt: The black rook is undefended. Take it!

mv-make-luft.prompt: Black threatens Rd1#. Push a pawn to give your king an escape square.
mv-make-luft.explanation: For example h3: the king gets "luft" on h2 and is safe from back-rank mates.

tactic-zwischenzug.explanation: Instead of the expected move (like a recapture), you first insert a stronger one, usually a check or threat.

choices.inBetween: A stronger move inserted before the expected one

tactic-overload.explanation: A piece with two defensive jobs at once — attack one and the other collapses.

choices.twoJobs: It must guard two things at once

tactic-decoy.explanation: A sacrifice that lures an enemy piece (often the king or queen) onto a bad square.

choices.lure: Luring an enemy piece onto a bad square

tactic-windmill.explanation: A repeated series of discovered checks, with the moving piece grabbing material each time.

choices.repeatDiscovered: Repeated discovered checks that keep winning material

tactic-greek-gift.prompt: The bishop sacrifice on h7 (Bxh7+) against a castled king is known as what?

tactic-desperado.explanation: A piece that is lost anyway, so it grabs as much as it can before being taken.

choices.doomed: A doomed piece that sells itself dearly

tactic-trapped-piece.explanation: An attacked piece whose every escape square is unsafe — it will be lost.

choices.noSquares: It has no safe square to go to
choices.pinned: It is pinned to the king

tactic-remove-defender.explanation: Capture or trade off the piece guarding something important, then attack what it was guarding.

choices.removeGuard: Eliminate the guard, then hit what it guarded

tactic-cct.prompt: When looking for tactics, in what order should you check moves?
tactic-cct.explanation: Checks → captures → threats: the most forcing moves first.

tactic-sacrifice.explanation: Giving up material on purpose for something bigger: mate, more material, or a strong attack.

choices.giveForGain: Giving material on purpose for a bigger gain

tactic-royal-fork.prompt: A fork of the king and queen at the same time is often called what?
tactic-royal-fork.explanation: A "royal fork" — it almost always wins the queen.

tactic-relative-pin.prompt: A piece is "relatively" pinned (a queen behind it, not the king). May it move?
tactic-relative-pin.explanation: Yes — the move is legal, but you will usually lose the piece behind it.

choices.canMove: Yes, but usually at a cost

tactic-skewer-vs-pin.prompt: How is a skewer different from a pin?
tactic-skewer-vs-pin.explanation: In a skewer the more valuable piece is in front and must move, exposing the one behind.

choices.frontValuable: Skewer: the valuable piece is in front
choices.backValuable: Skewer: the valuable piece is behind

tactic-discovered-check-power.prompt: Why is a discovered check usually so powerful?
tactic-discovered-check-power.explanation: The opponent must deal with the check, so the piece that moved can do anything — like grab the queen.

choices.freeMove: The moving piece gets a free action

tactic-perpetual.explanation: A draw — the position repeats three times. A great way to save a lost game.

choices.win: A win for the checking side
choices.lose: A loss for the checking side

tactic-stalemate-trick.prompt: A side that is badly losing (king and few pieces) can look for a draw through what?
tactic-stalemate-trick.explanation: A stalemate trick: give away the last pieces so your king has no move but is not in check.

tactic-luft.explanation: An escape square made by pushing a pawn in front of the king, against back-rank mates.

choices.escapeSquare: An escape square made by a pawn push
